newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro says socialism goes on despite pressure.
newsitem.headline: Castro says socialism goes on despite pressure.

text.p: Veteran Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro, likening his people to the early Christians persecuted in ancient Rome, said on Tuesday his island was a socialist success story despite the "evil" of a U.S. blockade.

The 70-year-old president, who earlier held an historic audience with Pope John Paul at the Vatican, rejected calls for him to implement democratic reforms in return for improved economic ties and vowed there would be no change of course.
"We are like Christians in ancient Rome before Christianity was known," Castro told a news conference. "They resisted and we will resist. They suffered for their ideology. We suffer."
He said socialism in the Caribbean island he has ruled for nearly 38 years could be "perfected", but added: "There is no going back. There is no instrumenting a counter-revolution in Cuba.
"I think the facts speak for themselves. We will continue along this path."
Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar has urged Castro to improve Cuba's human rights record and increase democracy in return for improved trade links with the European Union.
Castro needs friends in Europe since his island has been under an economic blockade by Washington for 34 years.

But the veteran Marxist leader hinted that Spain was meddling in Cuba's affairs. The island was a Spanish colony until 1898. "We're fine as we are," he said. "We don't want to have to have another war of independence against Spain."
He said he had rejected Aznar's approach when the two leaders met in Chile for a recent Iberoamerican summit, likening it to a game of chess.
"I told him that the destiny of a country is not worked out on a chessboard," Castro said.
Castro again blasted the U.S. blockade and the Helms-Burton law, which allows Cuban Americans to sue foreign firms or individuals who own or operate properties seized by Havana.
He said U.S. President Bill Clinton was no "guerrilla, but not a man of peace either. Clinton is the fruit of that society, that politics". But he saw no immediate end to the blockade.
"Let's have no illusions," Castro said. "We should rather trust in our capacity to fight, to resist and wait for it to pass. They say there is no evil which lasts 100 years."

Castro, displaying the same good humour and wit at the news conference as during last week's World Food Summit in Rome, where he stole the show and was treated like royalty, said he had never considered himself a celebrity.
"I consider myself a revolutionary," he said. "I consider myself a slave to duty which I have tried to fulfil with humility and honour."
